The Candle in the Window

The Impossible Cure
An ash fever strikes the farmers’ children. Lyra knows two cures: one slow and honest, one quick and made of blood.
The ash fever has passed, one way or another.
“A bearer. I can tell by the way you walk: like someone carrying a weight they don’t take off at night.” She dries a mug that’s already dry. “Sit down. The fire here is free. Nothing else is.”
Why do you keep a candle burning in the window?
Look at her more closely.
I just need news.
Her hands only tremble when she looks at the door. She hasn’t slept. Under the counter there’s a small travel bag, packed, that she doesn’t have the courage to use.
You’re waiting for someone. Who?
She just seems tired. Like everyone in the valley.
And the candle?
“News? Marcus is requisitioning even the nails. Vesper buys children with words. And there’s a soldier in Bertoldo’s barn who thinks nobody knows.” She lowers her voice. “Everybody knows.”
A soldier?
And the candle in the window?
“A deserter. Name’s Garrik. He only brings food to the children, and children don’t talk.” She shrugs. “If the Capital finds him, they’ll hang him and whoever hid him.”

The smile falls from her face. “Wren. My daughter. Seventeen and her head full of gravestones. She went down into the Cemetery of the Betrayed three nights ago: she said someone down there was calling her name.” For the first time she truly looks at you. “You go down there. Bring her back to me.”
I’ll find her. I promise.
What’s in it for me?
Pay me first. Grief isn’t a currency.
I can’t promise anything.
“Everything I have is behind this counter.” She pushes a pouch toward you. “Ash. And my silence, when the Capital asks questions.”
I accept. I’ll find Wren.
Keep it. I just need to know what was calling her name.
She laughs without joy. “I’ve seen bigger men than you cry in that chair.” But she pushes the pouch over anyway. “Take it. And bring her home.”
All right.
She swallows. She empties the drawer without counting. “This is a lifetime of savings. Bring her back alive and I’ll forgive you.”
Deal.
“She said it was a woman’s voice, under the gravestones. That it promised to ‘keep the names warm’.” She shivers. “On the third floor there’s a nameless crypt. That’s where she left her red ribbon.”
I’ll go all the way down.
“Thank you.” It’s only a word, but she says it like someone who hasn’t used it in years. “Go beyond the third floor. She’ll be where the names are freshest.”
I’m going.
“Nothing?” she asks before you open your mouth. The candle is shorter than yesterday.
Not yet. I’ll go deeper.
Tell me about Wren again.
Orsola stands so fast she knocks over the stool. “You saw her. I can read it in your eyes. Is she… is she alive?”
She’s alive. She chose to stay with the Gravediggers, but she sends you this ribbon.
You told Orsola the truth: Wren stayed among the graves.
She’s right outside. I brought her home.
You brought Wren back to her mother.
She’s dead. She didn’t suffer. (Lie, so as not to break her heart twice)
You told Orsola that Wren was dead.
I handed her over to the Lady of the Gravestones. It was the price of passage.
You sold Wren to the Lady of the Gravestones.

She takes the red ribbon with two fingers, as if it were glass. She cries and laughs at once. “She always chose for herself. Who do you think she got that from?” She blows out the candle. “At least now I know where to look when I miss her.”
She’ll be safe down there.
The door opens. Wren walks in, covered in dirt, the ribbon in her hand. Nobody says anything for a very long time. Then Orsola hugs her so hard the girl laughs. “The inn is yours, bearer. Forever.”
Light another candle. To celebrate.
She believes you. She sits down slowly. “At least she didn’t suffer.” She pinches out the candle without feeling the heat. She will never light it again.
“Liar.” She says it without anger. “You have the eyes of someone who saw her alive.” She turns to the window. “If she chose not to come back, tell me. I already tell myself enough lies.”
You’re right. She’s alive, and she chose the graves.
Orsola doesn’t scream. She takes a knife from under the counter, looks at it, puts it back. “Get out. And never come back to my inn.” From that day on, the candle in the window is black.
“Beer? News? A chair by the fire?” Orsola makes room for you without asking anything.
Any news in the valley?
A rusty blade grazes your throat before your eyes adjust to the dark of the barn. “One step and I’ll split you like a sack of grain.” The voice shakes more than the blade.
Lower the weapon. If I wanted you hanged, I’d have brought Marcus.
Try it. I’ve seen worse than you under the Cemetery.
I brought you food. (Show the supplies)
Sorry. Wrong barn.
The blade nicks your skin. A drop of blood. Then he lowers it on his own, exhausted. “I can’t keep threatening people. What do you want?”
To talk.
Garrik backs up against the wall and drops the sword. “Fine. Fine. I’m no hero. I never was.”
Then tell me what you are.

“Garrik. Third regiment of the Capital. The night of the portal they ordered us to bar the doors of the upper village. With the people inside.” He looks at his hands. “I opened one door. Just one. Then I ran. To them I’m a deserter. To me… I don’t know what I am.”
You saved lives. I’ll help you escape.
Who gave that order?
Marcus would pay well for you.
I was there. I saw you open that door.
Garrik stares at you for a long time. Then he drops to his knees. “Then I didn’t dream it. Then someone got out alive.” He grips your hand with both of his. “Whatever you need. Anything.”
I need you to live. I’ll help you escape.
“A seal I’d never seen before. Not the Capital’s. A closed eye, sewn shut with black thread.” He lowers his voice. “The Market Shadows. Someone in Hondovalle wanted the upper village to burn.”
I’ll find out. Meanwhile, I’ll help you escape.
I’ll think about it.
“Then do it.” He doesn’t run. “But remember that night you also chose who to let burn.”
No. I’ll help you.
“Beyond the northern passes there’s a village that’s never heard of the Capital. I need forty rations to get there alive.” He hesitates. “And someone to distract Marcus’s patrols.”
Here are the supplies. Go, tonight.
You helped Garrik escape beyond the passes.
I’ll come back when I have them.
Garrik has been sharpening the same blade for hours. “Have you decided what to do with me?”
I’ll help you escape.
Yes. Come with me to Marcus.
You handed Garrik over to the Capital.
Not yet.
“The patrols are closing in. A few more nights and they’ll find me on their own.”
I’ll talk to Marcus: I’ll tell him you died in the Swamps.
You convinced Marcus that Garrik was dead.
Stay and fight for Hondovalle. The village needs a sword.
Garrik stayed to defend Hondovalle.
I’m working on it.
Marcus listens to your story, writes “dead, Swamps” and closes the ledger. That night Garrik leaves without looking back. On the barn door you find a cleaned sword and a note: “A door for a door.”
Marcus looks at you for a long time. “Strange. The Swamps never return the tags.” He nods to two soldiers. That night the barn burns. Garrik doesn’t come out.
Garrik loads the rations without a word. At the threshold he stops. “A door for a door, bearer.” He leaves you his old sword, cleaned for the first time in months.
Safe travels.
Garrik doesn’t resist. As the soldiers drag him away, he looks at you only once. Marcus pays you in new coins. They weigh more than they should.
Garrik takes off his burned uniform and throws it into the fire. “Then Hondovalle it is.” From that night on, the watchtowers have one more man who never sleeps.
Welcome home.
Garrik nods to you from the barn. He seems almost at peace.

A woman with bandaged eyes traces lines on an enormous parchment. She stops before you speak. “You walk like someone who’s been down in the Cemetery. Turn left on the second floor next time. On the right there’s someone who knows you.”
How do you know where I’ve been?
Your maps… change on their own. They’re bound to the Seals of Krak.
“I listen. Every choice in the valley makes a sound, like a stone in a well. Roads shift toward whoever chooses.” She touches the paper. “You make a lot of noise, bearer.”
What are you drawing now?

She smiles for the first time. “Few understand that. The Wardens built the Seals on top of the Heart’s roads. To draw the roads is to know where the Seals give way.” She hands you a sheet. “You’ll need this.”
Thank you. Can I help you?

“In the Swamps of Vhalzareth there’s a path I can’t hear. As if someone were keeping it silent.” She turns her head toward you. “Go down at least to the third floor. When you find it, the path will speak to you. Come back and tell me.”
I will.
What’s in it for me?
Not now.
“A place on my map. Whoever ends up on it, the valley doesn’t forget.” A pause. “And a Warden relic, if you really want something you can touch.”
I accept.
“The Swamps are still silent to me. Third floor, bearer. At least.”
I’m on my way.
Sibilla stiffens. “I can hear it on you. You’ve walked the mute path.” She brings her face close to yours, as if to smell you. “What was at the end?”
A Cult altar, built on top of a broken Seal.
There was nothing. And that was the point: someone erased the road.
I found nothing. (Keep the secret and sell it to the Shadows)
“The Cult drinks from the broken Seals.” She draws a red line on the paper. “Now that it’s drawn, the Wardens will know where to strike.”
Then the valley breathes a little easier.
You revealed to Sibilla the altar on the broken Seal.

Sibilla goes still. “Erased. You don’t erase a road: you erase the memory of those who knew it.” She removes the bandage: behind it there are no eyes, only scars shaped like a seal. “Then whoever burned the upper village wanted something forgotten. Don’t stop looking.”
I won’t.
You discovered that someone erased one of Krak’s roads.
Sibilla nods slowly. “Pity.” She doesn’t insist. Later, Varo the merchant pays you very well for a path nobody else knows.
You sold the secret of the Swamps to the Shadows.
“You’re lying.” She says it gently. “Lies make a shrill sound on paper.” She turns her back to you. “Come back when you want to tell me the truth.”
All right. There was a Cult altar.
Sibilla draws. Without raising her head: “Your road has changed again. Be careful.”

An elegant man, too elegant for Hondovalle, tips his hat. “Varo, at your service. I buy what you no longer need: the taste of an apple, the name of a friend, the day you were afraid.” He waves a vial full of light. “Honest prices. More or less.”
You buy… memories?
The Market Shadows. The sewn eye: it’s your seal.

Varo’s smile doesn’t move, but his eyes do. “You know too much for someone carrying a single Burden.” He leans in. “Not all Shadows think alike. I, for one, don’t burn villages. Terrible for business.”
Then who did it?
“Someone who wanted the valley to forget a road. Ask the blind cartographer.” He presses a bone coin into your hand. “And consider this a down payment on your discretion.”
I accept the coin.
Keep your money.

“There’s a boy, Pip. He sold me the memory of his mother for a slice of cake. A bargain for both of us.” He shows a warm, golden vial. “Now the mother cries, and the boy calls her ‘ma’am’. Want to buy it back? Six hundred ash. For you.”
I’ll buy it back.
You bought back Pip’s memory.
He’s a child. Give it back and the valley will remember you as a man of honor.
Give me the vial or I’ll open you like one of your bottles.
Cut the strap of his bag while he talks.
It’s none of my business.
“Ah, principles.” Varo puts the vial away. “Come back when you have principles and six hundred ash. The two rarely travel together.”
Varo looks at you for a long time. Then he laughs. “Honor. Such an old-fashioned currency.” He tosses you the vial. “Tell him it’s from a stranger. I hate being thanked.”
You convinced Varo to return Pip’s memory.
Varo’s smile finally cracks. He hands you the vial with two fingers. “The Shadows don’t forget who threatens them, bearer. It’s literally our trade.”
Then let them remember.
You took Pip’s memory back with threats.
The vial slips into your hand without a sound. Varo keeps talking for a good minute before he notices. When he does, he slowly applauds. “Nice hands. You’re wasted on heroics.”
You stole Pip’s memory from Varo.
A gloved hand stops your wrist. “How rude.” Varo sighs. “The price just went up. Eight hundred.”
“Little Pip’s memory is still here. It’s getting cold, you know. Unsold memories age badly.”
I have a better memory to offer you. (Sell him a fake memory)
I’ll sell you one of my real memories in exchange.
You gave one of your memories to save Pip’s.

Varo uncorks your vial and sniffs. His eyes well up. “A mother singing in a kitchen that never existed. Magnificent. Fake, but magnificent.” He hands you Pip’s, laughing. “You tricked me. I appreciate it.”
You fooled Varo with a fake memory.
Varo presses an empty vial to your temple. You feel something leave: a summer afternoon, a laugh. You no longer know whose. “An honest trade,” Varo says quietly, for once not smiling.
That evening Pip runs across the square shouting “Mom!” as if for the first time. For him, it is.
It was worth it.
“Memories to sell? No? Pity. You have a face full of interesting things.”

A barefoot girl sits on the edge of the well, her feet over the void. She sings without opening her mouth. When she sees you, she stops. “You chose on the night of the portal,” she says in three different voices. “He heard you.”
Who? Who heard me?
Look at her carefully. Does she have a shadow?
Get down from the well. You’ll hurt yourself.
She has no shadow. Her shadow is the valley itself: when she moves, the cracks in the ground move with her. A shiver runs down your spine.
Who are you?

“Krak.” She says it the way you’d say “grandpa”. “He has no mouth, so he uses mine. He’s tired. Everyone who goes down brings him a burden and leaves it on top of him.” She tilts her head. “Want to hear his song? A verse is missing.”
Sing it.
Krak isn’t a god. He’s a memory. A memory that forgot it was alive.
Not today.

“Beneath the well sleeps one with no name / they gave him a thousand burdens as gifts / each one weighed like a choice…” She stops abruptly. “Then I don’t remember. The verse is in the Tower of Silence, where people stop speaking. Will you bring it to me?”
I’ll bring it to you.
What happens if I complete the song?
“Krak remembers his name.” She smiles, and for an instant her teeth are stone. “And whoever remembers their name can choose.”

The three voices fall silent. Only one remains, a child’s. “No one has ever understood that so soon.” She takes your hand: it’s cold as a gravestone. “Then bring the verse. Together we’ll remind him.”
Nym hums the song up to where it breaks off. Then starts again. Then starts again.
I’m looking for the verse.
Nym jumps down from the well before you arrive. “You have it on you. The verse. Sing it.”
“…and the first burden was his own name / which he gave to the valley to keep it alive.”
Invent a different verse: one that keeps him asleep.

The ground trembles. Every crack in Hondovalle glows for an instant. Nym cries with eyes of stone. “He was called Krak because they took the rest of his name. He gave it to the valley to keep it alive. And we buried him under our burdens.” She looks at you. “Now you know. In the end, you’ll be able to choose whether to give it back.”
You completed the Underground Song. Krak remembers having been someone.

Your verse is sweet and convincing. The ground stops trembling. Nym yawns, curls up on the edge of the well and falls asleep. When you come back the next day, she’s gone. The valley is calmer. And emptier.
You put Krak back to sleep with a false song.
Before you speak, Nym turns to Kael. “Your brother has cold feet,” she says. “He’s sitting on the other side of the portal, counting the days. He isn’t alive. But he isn’t finished either.”
Is there a way to bring him back?
“No.” Simple, cruel, childlike. “But there’s a way to say goodbye. When the Heart stops, the portal will open one last time. One of you will be able to talk to him.”
I’ll tell Kael.
Nym plays with a pebble that falls into the well and comes back up on its own. “He’s listening,” she says, without looking at you.

Kael stokes the fire with the tip of his sword. He doesn’t look at you. “Every night I dream Tomas knocks at the door. Every night I open it, and there’s no one.” A spark lands on his hand. He doesn’t shake it off. “Tell me the truth. Do you think he’s still alive, on the other side?”
I pushed him. I won’t lie to you: I don’t know what’s on the other side.
I don’t know. But we’ll find out together.
Tomas chose to stand near the seal. He was brave. Honor him by living.
He’s dead, Kael. Get over it.

Kael is silent for a long time. “I knew. That it was you.” He grips his sword. Then he plants it in the ground and leans on it. “Thank you for not hiding it from me. It’s the first true thing anyone has told me since that night.”
Then let’s look for the truth. Together.
“Together.” He repeats the word as if tasting it. “All right. But if I find out you lied to me, bearer, the next burden you carry will be my sword.”
That’s fair.
Kael lowers his head. “Brave. Yes. He was always the first to jump into the river.” He smiles, barely. “All right. I’ll live. But I want to know what’s beyond that portal.”
We’ll find out.
Kael gets up and moves to the other side of the fire. He doesn’t say a word for the rest of the night. When you wake up, he’s already stood watch alone.
“Any news of Tomas?” Kael asks every evening, pretending it’s a question like any other.
Not yet. There’s a girl at the well who seems to know things she shouldn’t.

You tell him about Nym. About the portal that will open one last time. Kael listens without interrupting. At the end, he looks at the flames. “Not alive. But not finished.” He laughs softly, and it’s the first time you’ve heard him laugh. “That’s just like him.”
When the portal opens, you’ll be the one to speak to him.
Kael will be able to say goodbye to Tomas.
I’ll speak to him. I have to ask his forgiveness.
You and Kael will speak to Tomas together.
“Thank you.” Kael holds out his hand. It isn’t forgiveness, not yet. But it’s the closest thing to it.
“We’ll speak to him together,” Kael says. “He’ll have something to say to both of us.” For the first time, he sits beside you instead of across from you.
Kael cleans his blade. “We go down tomorrow? Good. This time stay behind me.”

Lyra’s hands are black up to the wrists. “Ash fever. Six children, at the Bertoldo farm. They breathe like broken bellows.” She sits down heavily. “Elara has a cure. Slow, safe, expensive. And then there’s the other one.”
What other one?
Tell me what you need.
“Blood from the Font. One drop per child and the fever is gone in an hour.” She looks down. “And for the rest of their lives they’ll hear the Font calling them. The Cult will consider them its own.”
Let’s do the slow cure. I’ll get you what you need.
A drop of blood isn’t a sentence. I know that well.
The children were healed with the Font’s blood.
Use the blood. Six living children are worth a calling.
“Twenty supplies for the broths and a hundred ash for Elara’s herbs. Every day we wait, a child gets worse.”
Here they are.
You paid for the slow cure: all the children recovered.
I’ll find them.
“Two children are breathing better. Four aren’t.” Lyra doesn’t look up from the mortar. “Do you have the supplies?”
Use the Font’s blood. There’s no more time.

Three days later, six children are chasing chickens in the Bertoldo yard. Lyra watches them with shining eyes. “You know what Elara taught me? That sometimes the right cure is simply the one that costs you the most.” She rests her head on your shoulder, just for a moment.

Within an hour the fever is gone. Six children sleep peacefully. On the nape of each neck, a small red drop-shaped mark. Lyra washes the vials in silence, three times, even though they’re already clean.
Lyra checks your wounds without asking permission. “Still breathing. Good. Keep it up.”
The Nameless Crypt

A red ribbon tied to a gravestone. Beyond it, a candlelit crypt: hooded figures dust carved names. One of them turns around. It’s a girl, with Orsola’s eyes. “I’m not lost,” says Wren. “Down here someone remembers the dead. Up there nobody even remembers the living.” Behind her, a Lady made of dust watches you.
Your mother has kept a candle burning for three nights. Come home with me.
Wren hesitates for a long time. Then she unties the ribbon from the gravestone. “Just to say goodbye to her properly.” She follows you toward the surface.
You’ve chosen. I respect your choice. I’ll bring the ribbon to your mother.
Wren puts the ribbon in your hand. “Tell her I’m fine. Tell her it’s warm here.” The Lady of dust bows her head to you.
Leave her to the Lady of the Gravestones in exchange for safe passage.
The Lady smiles with a mouth full of earth. Wren doesn’t understand at first. When she does, it’s already too late.
The Funeral Without a Body
The farmers are burying an empty coffin: a man lost in the Swamps. The widow asks you to say a few words, because “bearers speak with the dead”. Vesper listens from nearby.
Tell the truth: no one knows where he is.
Your words are simple and true. The widow nods, grateful. Someone finally cries.
Tell of a heroic death that never happened.
The village will have a hero. The widow will have a story. You’ll have one more lie to carry.
Let Vesper speak.
Vesper speaks of the Font that welcomes everyone. That night, two families light a red candle.
The Tavern Challenge
At Orsola’s inn a Capital mercenary challenges anyone to arm-wrestle. He’s already won three times and is insulting the farmers. Orsola looks at you as if to say: “Do something.”
Accept the challenge.
It’s a long, brutal duel. You win by a hair. The tavern erupts in a roar. The mercenary buys you a drink, like a good sport.
Bet against the farmers.
You win a tidy sum. Orsola serves you the lukewarmest beer in the valley.
Whisper to the mercenary that his mother is looking for him at the door.
He runs outside. There’s no one there. When he comes back, the whole tavern is laughing at him. He leaves without finishing his beer.
